title: Ping Pong Diplomacy
text:
In April 1971 the World Table Tennis Championships were held in Nagoya, Japan. The United States and the People's Republic of China had had no diplomatic relations for over twenty years, and Chinese players had been told to be careful about contact with Americans.

One day the American player Glenn Cowan, a free-spirited nineteen-year-old, missed his team's bus and climbed onto the bus of the Chinese team. There was an awkward silence. Then Zhuang Zedong, China's three-time world champion, came over, spoke to him through an interpreter and gave him a gift, a silk-screen picture of the Huangshan mountains. Photographers captured the two together as they got off the bus. The next day Cowan gave Zhuang a T-shirt in return.

The moment made headlines. In Beijing, Mao Zedong, who was already looking for a way to open contact with the United States, approved inviting the American team to China. Within days the team became the first official American group to visit the country since 1949. Premier Zhou Enlai received them in the Great Hall of the People and told them they had opened a new chapter in the relations between the two peoples.

In July 1971 Henry Kissinger made a secret trip to Beijing, and in February 1972 President Nixon visited China.
lesson: When a direct approach is too risky, a small, low-stakes gesture can test the water and let both sides move without losing face.
people: Glenn Cowan, Zhuang Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Mao Zedong
source: Contemporary press reports; Zhuang Zedong's later interviews; Nicholas Griffin, Ping-Pong Diplomacy (2014)
